title: Foreground/Background Eviction Policy Simulation Notes
content:
Purpose and context:

This is a working note capturing a set of micro-simulations and short lab runs aimed at understanding tradeoffs between a two-tier eviction policy (foreground vs background) and its impact on:
- token-level generation latency (p50/p95)
- KV cache reuse rates (per-request and aggregated)
- paging events and NVMe spillback frequency
- memory bandwidth saturation and host-side stalls

We are trying to reproduce a realistic multi-tenant workload with a mix of short chat-turns (seqlen 32–128) and long completions (seqlen 512–2k). The hypothesis is that separating eviction responsibility into a cheap foreground eviction for immediate pressure and a slower background coalescing pass can reduce tail latencies while keeping resident set relevant.

Experiment summary (what we ran):

1) Simulator + synthetic traces
- Trace sources: sample traces from production sampling (~2 hours of requests across 50 tenants) + synthetic long-tail generator (zipf alpha=1.2 for key popularity).
- Simulator modeled: per-key metadata (last_access_ts, reuse_count, size_in_pages), KV residency bitmap, page-level mapping (4KB pages), and host NVMe spillback latency distribution (P50=4ms, P95=11ms, P99=50ms).
- Eviction policies tested: LRU (baseline), recency+size score (score = alpha*age + beta*size), foreground-first (evict smallest hot candidates immediately), and two-stage (foreground reclaim threshold + background coalesce with weighted decay).
- Metrics captured: reuse_rate (fraction of requests that hit resident KV entries), eviction_rate (entries/sec), average_pages_spilled/sec, and tail latency for token generation pipeline (simulated cost model: resident token cost = 0.25ms, fetched-from-disk cost = spillback_latency + 0.25ms).

2) Microbench on dev cluster (x8 A100-equivalent hosts)
- Real binary with instrumentation: lightweight counters (per-shard resident size), CUPTI-based kernel overlap measurements, and a prometheus endpoint for eviction events.
- Workloads: mixed synthetic (as above) and a replay of 30 minutes of sampled production traffic.
- Measured host memory bandwidth using nvprof and perf counters to observe correlation between peak bandwidth (>85%) and increase in paging events.

Key observations (simulator):

- Baseline LRU reproduces expected hotspot behavior: top 2% of keys account for ~45% of hits. However, long sequences cause transient hotset shifts: during long-completion bursts, access pattern drifts and LRU thrashes older long-tail items back in.

- Two-stage policy (foreground reclaim threshold set to 85% of cache; background pass runs at 10% CPU budget) improved p95 token latency by ~18% versus baseline in synthetic runs with high long-completion ratio. p50 changed <2%. Reuse_rate improved by +4–7 percentage points depending on zipf skew.

- Foreground-first (evict smallest-first to free pages quickly) reduced immediate page-fault spikes but increased average pages_spilled/sec by ~9% in long-run traces; the reason appears to be that preferring many small evictions evicts more keys overall (higher churn) which later lead to re-fetches.

- Weighted recency+size scoring reduced total bytes spilled compared to pure recency at a modest cost to reuse_rate for tiny keys. Tuning factor: beta (size weight) tested at 0.1–2.0; best observed tradeoff around beta=0.45 for our traces.

Microbench findings (real binary):

- When host memory bandwidth utilization crossed ~80% for sustained >200ms windows, we observed NVMe spillback latency amplification: p95 spill latency went from 11ms -> 28ms. This correlates with kernel-level DMA contention (observed via perf). In these windows, eviction pressure had outsized impact on generation tail latency.

- Background coalesce threads that perform batch eviction (moving groups of victims) cause short bursts of PCIe DMA that overlap with H2D model transfer windows; in our runs, moving the background pass to a lower core affinity (avoid cores used by model memcpy threads) reduced overlap and lowered p99 latency spikes.

- Enabling small, opportunistic prefetch cache (prefetch small KV fragments likely to be referenced next-turn) gave marginal benefit in high skew traces (+2% reuse) but hurt bandwidth in heavy multi-tenant mixes. Prefetch should be gated by per-shard BW headroom.

Representative numbers (dev cluster, replayed 30m):
- Baseline LRU: reuse_rate=72%, p50_token=6.8ms, p95_token=38.4ms, pages_spilled/sec=12.7
- Two-stage (85% fg threshold): reuse_rate=76%, p50=6.9ms, p95=31.4ms, pages_spilled/sec=10.9
- Foreground-small-first: reuse_rate=70%, p50=6.6ms, p95=35.0ms, pages_spilled/sec=13.8
- Recency+size (beta=0.45): reuse_rate=74%, p50=6.8ms, p95=33.0ms, pages_spilled/sec=9.6

Interpretation & root causes: 

- Tail latency is dominated by two interactions: (1) eviction-induced NVMe fetches (paging) and (2) contention on memory bandwidth and PCIe DMA during background maintenance. Reducing overall pages_spilled/sec and desynchronizing DMA from model H2D transfers reduce p95/p99 most.

- Small-key churn: policies that prioritize freeing little fragments to immediately satisfy memory pressure increase churn because they fail to account for the cost of refetching and the statistical reuse of those small keys. Size-awareness reduces bytes spilled and improves long-term reuse.

- Background coalescing is useful but must be BW-aware and core-affinity-aware. Running the coalesce worker on a CPU/core set that overlaps with memcpy kernels is a common source of tail spikes.

Practicals / heuristics to try in next sprint (actionable):

1) Implement a bandwidth-aware eviction budget: maintain a moving average of PCIe DMA throughput and throttle background eviction when avg_BW > 75%. Backoff should be exponential to avoid flip-flopping.

2) Two-tier scoring: compute score = w_recency*age_norm + w_size*size_norm + w_reuse*(1 - reuse_norm). Default weights: w_recency=0.5, w_size=0.3, w_reuse=0.2. Normalize per-shard. Evaluate sensitivity to weight shifts.

3) Foreground shortcut for emergency pressure: a constant-time ring of candidate victims maintained by recent insertion; only used when resident_size > hard_limit and only evict up to X pages per request to avoid large per-request stalls.

4) Background coalesce placement: pin background eviction to a low-priority core set and ensure its work is spread (batch size cap) so background DMA is small and frequent instead of large bursts. Add an observer to the model H2D queue to avoid co-location.

5) Metrics instrumentation: expose per-shard counters for pages_evicted_by_policy, pages_reclaimed_by_foreground, background_eviction_bw_bytes and a histogram of background_eviction_batch_size. Add alerts when background_eviction_bw_bytes / total_nvme_bw > 0.3.

Open questions / risks:

- How to tune weights across tenants with very different working set sizes? A single global weighting will underperform for tiny-shard (low memory) customers. We might need shard-level auto-tuning.

- Prefetch gating: what is the right headroom signal? GPU H2D queue depth vs measured PCIe BW? Need an experiment to correlate.

- Hardware variability: NVMe tail behavior changes by drive model (SAS vs NVMe, vendor queuing). Need cross-hardware runs before shipping any default settings.

Next experiments to run (tickets):

- RT-1010: Bandwidth-aware eviction budget simulation (simulate exponential backoff).
- RT-1011: Background worker core-affinity experiment on staging (pin to isolated cpus).
- RT-1012: Shard-level auto-tuner: short RL/heuristic to pick w_size per shard based on measured reuse curve (8h trial window).

Notes to reviewers:

- This doc mixes simulator outputs and real binary runs. The absolute numbers are environment-dependent; focus on qualitative behavior and relative deltas.

- Attached artifacts: sim CSVs (sims/fg-bg-sweep-2025-01-10.csv), perf flamegraphs (perf/flame-2025-01-23.svg) and a microbench prometheus snapshot (prom/eviction-snapshot-2025-01-29.json). Links above in linked_artifacts and in the ticket descriptions.

Takeaway (short):

A two-stage eviction approach with size-awareness + bandwidth-aware background eviction yields the best tradeoff for mixed seqlen workloads: reduces pages spilled and substantially improves tail latency (p95) without hurting p50. Next steps are to harden the BW gating and implement shard-level weight auto-tuning.

-- Ethan
